Sequential Decision Framework

Sequential decision problems require decisions under uncertainty and evolving information. Powell’s framework decomposes each period into three parts: the state S, a decision X, and new information W. This cycle repeats over time.

State St

Aggregated cost, schedule, carbon, temperature
→

Decision Xt

Scope & budget shifts (quarterly)
→

Info Wt+1

Temperature deviation + shocks

Reference: Powell (Sequential Decision Analytics & Modeling). [1]

Modeling Variables & Policies

Variables

  • State S: aggregated metrics (cost, schedule, carbon)
  • Decision X: scope & budget adjustments each quarter
  • Exogenous W: temperature deviations from trend
Policy & action set used in the simulation (click to expand)

Each quarter we select an action (scope_shift, budget_shift) in [−1, +1] × [−1, +1].

Policy A: Random baseline

Uniform random actions in [−1, +1].

Policy B: Cautious heuristic

State‑responsive budget/scope rules (schedule & carbon thresholds).

The plots in this brief correspond to the cautious heuristic policy.

Powell’s solution / policy classes

  1. Policy Function Approximations (PFA)
  2. Cost Function Approximations (CFA)
  3. Approximate Dynamic Programming (ADP)
  4. Policy search & reinforcement learning

Reference: Powell (Unified framework / SDAM). [1]

RL vs Powell: Comparison

Reinforcement Learning

  • State (s): environment representation
  • Action (a): decision taken by agent
  • Reward (r): immediate feedback signal
  • Transition: st+1 = T(st, at) + noise
  • Goal: maximise expected cumulative reward

Powell’s Framework

  • State (S): knowledge + physical system
  • Decision (X): action chosen by manager
  • Exogenous info (W): new data & shocks
  • Transition: St+1 = f(St, Xt, Wt+1)
  • Goal: maximise objective (e.g. minimise cost)

Key message: both are compatible — Powell’s notation is often clearer for project governance. [1]

Project Scenario: Climate Mega‑Project

  • 25‑year horizon (100 quarters)
  • Goal: deliver a climate intervention while controlling cost, schedule & carbon
  • Exogenous W: deviations in global mean temperature trend
  • Decisions X: quarter‑by‑quarter scope & budget shifts
  • State S: aggregated cost, schedule delay & carbon emissions
Why “quarterly” as the timestep?

Quarterly is a natural executive governance cadence: funding decisions, scope gates, contracting changes, and updated climate indicators typically arrive on that rhythm. The simulator is designed to align decision cadence with the rate at which meaningful new information arrives.

Data & Assumptions

Parameters calibrate the simulator for a 25‑year mega‑project. The temperature trend is grounded in IPCC evidence, while other drifts and coefficients are illustrative to demonstrate how scope and budget choices affect cost, schedule and emissions.

Component Default value How it is used in the model
Baseline temperature trend 0.2°C / decade ≈ 0.005°C / quarter Sets the deterministic term in W each quarter.
Temperature noise σ = 0.02°C per quarter Additive Gaussian shock term in W (forecast/variability).
Baseline drifts cost +100/q; schedule +0/q; carbon +10/q Business‑as‑usual quarterly increments absent decisions & climate stress.
Decision coefficients cost = 150·scope + 50·budget
schedule = 0.5·scope − 0.3·budget
carbon = 8·scope − 2·budget 		Encodes trade‑offs: scope expands cost/schedule/carbon; budget increases spend but can accelerate & decarbonise.
Temperature sensitivities cost +20 per °C
schedule +0.2 per °C
carbon +1 per °C 		Hotter quarters cause extra cost, delay and emissions (stressors).
Noise std deviations cost 50; schedule 0.2; carbon 5 Unmodelled uncertainty (supply chain, tech surprises, execution variance).

Notes: values are abstract units. Replace with programme‑specific calibration once data is available. [2]

State Transition Model

Cost: St+1.cost = St.cost + C0 + αc·scope + βc·budget + γc·W + εc
Schedule: St+1.schedule = St.schedule + S0 + αs·scope + βs·budget + γs·W + εs
Carbon: St+1.carbon = St.carbon + Q0 + αq·scope + βq·budget + γq·W + εq
Temperature: temperaturet+1 = temperaturet + trend + noise

Linear update equations combine baseline drifts, decision effects, temperature deviations and noise. Coefficients (α, β, γ) determine how scope, budget and temperature influence each metric.

Implementation reference: climate_engineering_simulator.py. [2]

Simulation Methodology

1) Initialise

S0 = (0,0,0,0)
→

2) Observe

At quarter t, observe St
→

3) Decide

Apply policy π(t, St) → Xt
→

4) Evolve

Sample W + noise; update St+1
Algorithmic view (click to expand) 
for t in 0..T-1:
    observe S_t
    choose X_t = π(t, S_t)
    sample W_{t+1}
    S_{t+1} = f(S_t, X_t, W_{t+1}) + noise
repeat for many Monte‑Carlo paths

This is the core loop needed for Monte‑Carlo tree search evaluations. [1][2]

Sample Paths: Cost

  • Costs grow steadily over time across all scenarios.
  • Variation arises from random shocks and policy choices.
  • Careful budgeting can moderate cost escalation.

Trajectory plot generated from simulator under the cautious policy. [2]

Sample Paths: Schedule & Carbon

  • Schedule exhibits high variability; decisions & temperature drive delays.
  • Carbon emissions rise steadily; budget increases can dampen emissions.
  • Balanced policies are needed to manage trade‑offs.

Insights & Interpretation

  • Costs rise predictably but can be moderated through budget shifts.
  • Schedule overruns depend strongly on temperature deviations and scope choices.
  • Carbon emissions accumulate rapidly; proactive emission‑reduction measures pay off.
  • Uncertainty introduces wide dispersion: robust policies should perform well across scenarios.
What to do with this insight as a Project Director
  • Make quarterly decisions explicitly “robust”: evaluate not only the mean outcome but tail risks (p90 delay, p90 cost).
  • Separate actions (what teams do) from decisions (what the director approves) and from uncertainty reduction (what information to seek).
  • Use simulator outputs to structure governance conversations: “which uncertainty is driving dispersion?”

Recommendations & Strategies

  • Monitor temperature deviations quarterly and adjust scope/budget accordingly.
  • Invest additional budget when schedule lags; reduce scope when emissions spike.
  • Use Monte‑Carlo tree search to evaluate decision sequences and select robust actions.
  • Augment policies with reinforcement learning to learn from past data.
Example governance pattern (quarterly)
  1. Review updated W (temperature deviation) and execution KPIs.
  2. Run 200–1,000 rollouts under candidate actions (coarse discretisation is fine).
  3. Choose action that best meets objective (cost/schedule/carbon) and risk appetite.
  4. Assign “uncertainty reduction” actions: what must we measure/learn next quarter?

What this tool is (and isn’t)
  • Is: a fast, transparent executive simulator for sequential decision framing and policy stress testing.
  • Isn’t: a validated climate model or an earned‑value schedule engine.
  • Best use: define the governance “decision loop”, clarify what information (W) matters, and test policy robustness.

Conclusion & Next Steps

  • Powell’s framework clarifies state, decision and exogenous information for project management.
  • Simulations reveal wide uncertainty; decisions and temperature deviations shape project outcomes.
  • Monte‑Carlo tree search supports robust decision‑making under uncertainty.
  • Next: refine calibrations, integrate RL algorithms, build an interactive decision tool.
